title: Water a sprout: not too much, not too little
description: A tiny green sprout is thirsty — but did you know too much water can make it poorly? Learn the finger test that tells you exactly when your sprout wants a drink.

body.heading: The finger test
paragraphs: Plants drink water through their roots, down in the soil. The top of the soil can look dry while underneath it is still wet — so gardeners do not guess. They test.

Push your finger gently into the soil, about as deep as your fingernail. If soil sticks to your finger and feels damp, your sprout is happy — no drink today. If your finger comes out clean and dry, it is watering time.

body.heading: How to give a good drink
paragraphs: Pour water slowly onto the soil, not onto the leaves, and stop when a little water runs out of the hole in the bottom of the pot. That escaping water tells you the drink reached all the way down to the roots.

Then tip away any water sitting in the saucer after ten minutes. Roots that sit in puddles all day can rot, and a soggy sprout droops just like a thirsty one. Just enough, not too much — that is the sprout-keeper's secret.

takeaway: Use the finger test: damp soil means wait, dry soil means water slowly until a little runs out of the bottom — then empty the saucer.
ageGuidance: Ages 4–9, with a grown-up helping with water.
materials: A potted sprout or young plant
A small cup or watering can of water
supervision: A grown-up stays with the child while watering, helps carry the water, and checks the saucer is emptied afterwards.
safetyNotes: Wipe up spilled water straight away so nobody slips, and wash hands after touching soil.
Only water plants a grown-up says are safe to touch — some plants have prickles or leaves that should not be handled.
screenFreeExtension: Keep a rain diary for a week: draw a cup for every day it rains, and think about how outdoor plants get their drinks without any help from you.
